_comment: The Museum encyclopedia's explainers (ui-spec.md component 18, design.md 1.1): how things work, drawn as engineering sheets. Outside the frozen content pack, like strings.json, so text fixes reach running games. Each sheet has a drawing from assets/ui/explainers/ (made by assets-raw/explainers/make_explainer_art.py), three points, an 'In Launch Window' line, and optionally a legend and bars drawn by the client. Every figure is checked (design.md 1.1). No inline bold: a label can't switch fonts mid-text.

explainers.title: Suborbital vs orbital
explainers.summary: Why reaching space is easy and staying up is hard: Newton's cannon, two Mercury flights side by side, and the rocket equation.

sheets.title: Falling around the world

points.title: Space is close
points.text: The edge of space is only about 100 km up: an hour's drive, if you could drive straight up. Reaching it is the easy part. Go up, then fall straight back down. That's a suborbital flight.

points.title: Orbit means falling sideways
points.text: Anything you throw falls back down. Throw it faster and it lands farther away. Throw it fast enough and the ground curves away beneath it as quickly as it falls: it keeps falling, all the way around the Earth. That's an orbit.

points.title: The 8-kilometre rule
points.text: Earth's surface drops away about 5 metres for every 8 km you travel in a straight line. Anything you let go of falls about 5 metres in its first second. So travel 8 km every second, about 28,000 km/h, and you fall exactly as fast as the ground drops away.

sheets.inGame: The goal Human in space needs only a suborbital flight. Human in orbit needs the full 7.8 km/s, and a rocket that can lift your capsule to low Earth orbit.

sheets.title: Height isn't the hard part

points.title: Same capsule, similar height
points.text: In May 1961 a Mercury capsule carried Alan Shepard on a 15-minute suborbital hop. Nine months later the same kind of capsule carried John Glenn three times around the world. Glenn flew only a little higher. Drawn to scale, both flights skim just above the air.

points.title: The difference is speed
points.text: Glenn went about 3.4 times as fast. The energy of motion grows with the square of the speed, so every kilogram of his capsule carried about 12 times as much of it. The rocket had to supply all of it.

points.title: So orbit needs a much bigger rocket
points.text: Shepard's Redstone weighed about 30 tonnes at liftoff. Glenn needed an Atlas of about 120 tonnes, first built as an intercontinental missile. Yuri Gagarin had already orbited in April 1961 on the Soviet R-7, another missile turned launcher.

sheets.inGame: Crewed programs fly a suborbital configuration first, such as Vostok · Suborbital flight. The orbital one needs a stronger human-rated rocket, and its program goal pays twice the prestige.

sheets.title: The rocket's hardest bargain

points.title: Fuel to carry fuel
points.text: A rocket has to lift its own propellant, and the propellant that lifts that. In 1903 Konstantin Tsiolkovsky worked out the result: the propellant needed grows exponentially with the speed you want. Needing about 3.8 times the speed (counting what gravity and air take on the way up) raises the propellant share from 57% to 96%.

points.title: Why rockets come in stages
points.text: Tanks, engines and the crew all have to fit in the last 4%. That's barely possible in one piece, so orbital rockets throw weight away on the way up. Even the Atlas, with steel tank walls thinner than a coin, dropped two of its three main engines.

points.title: Getting home is harder too
points.text: A suborbital capsule falls back by itself. An orbit never ends on its own: a retrorocket must brake the capsule just enough to dip into the air. Then the air turns about 12 times as much energy into heat, and the heat shield has to survive it.

sheets.inGame: In the VAB, compare a rocket's Suborbital payload with its LEO payload: the same rocket lifts far less to orbit. On Vostok · Orbital flight, the Retrofire step is the brake that brings the capsule home.

explainers.title: Rendezvous
explainers.summary: Why a spacecraft brakes to catch up with another, and how crews learned to meet and dock in orbit.

sheets.title: Slow down to catch up

points.title: Lower orbits are faster
points.text: Gravity pulls harder close to the Earth, so a craft in a low orbit has to fly faster to keep falling around it, and it has a shorter way to go. The lower the orbit, the shorter the lap.

points.title: Speed up, and you fall behind
points.text: Fire your engine towards a craft ahead of you and the extra speed lifts you into a higher orbit. A higher orbit takes longer to go round, so the target pulls away. A pilot's instincts, trained in aircraft, say the opposite.

points.title: Brake to catch up
points.text: To close the gap, you brake. The lower, quicker orbit gains a few minutes on every lap. Once you're just below the target, burn forward to rise and match its orbit.

sheets.inGame: Every Retrofire step uses the same idea. Braking lowers the orbit; on the far side of the Earth it dips into the air, and the craft comes home.

sheets.title: Learning to meet in orbit

points.title: Close isn't together
points.text: In August 1962 Vostok 3 and 4 passed within about 6.5 km, but neither could change its orbit, and they drifted apart. In June 1965 Gemini 4 tried to fly up to its own spent upper stage by pointing at it and thrusting. The stage only seemed to slip away, and the crew gave up to save fuel.

points.title: “Dr. Rendezvous”
points.text: In 1963 an Air Force pilot named Buzz Aldrin finished a doctorate at MIT on steering to a rendezvous by eye: hold the target still against the background stars, and correct whenever it drifts. On Gemini 12, in 1966, his radar failed, and he worked the approach out by hand with a sextant and charts.

points.title: Then came docking
points.text: Gemini 6A and 7 met in December 1965 and flew as close as about 30 cm. Gemini 8 made the first docking in March 1966; two uncrewed Soviet craft, Kosmos 186 and 188, docked automatically in 1967. The Moon landings depended on it: the lander had to find its command ship again in lunar orbit.

sheets.inGame: The goal Two crews together asks only for two craft within a few kilometres, which well-timed launches can manage, as Vostok 3 and 4 did. A real rendezvous needs a craft that can change its own orbit.

explainers.title: Going to the Moon
explainers.summary: The trip to the Moon priced in speed changes, and why the rocket that pays for it is so big.

sheets.title: The speed bill for the Moon

points.title: Orbit is halfway
points.text: Reaching low Earth orbit costs about 9.4 km/s of speed change, counting what gravity and air take on the way up. A saying credited to the writer Robert Heinlein puts it neatly: once you're in orbit, you're halfway to anywhere.

points.title: Every stop costs speed
points.text: Leaving Earth orbit for the Moon takes about 3.1 km/s more. The Moon has no air, so slowing into orbit around it, landing, climbing back up and setting off for home must all be done with rockets, and every one of those rockets has to be carried there first.

points.title: The air is free
points.text: The way home is the cheap part. Earth's atmosphere does the braking that would otherwise need another big rocket; a returning crew pays for it with a heat shield and parachutes instead of fuel.

sheets.inGame: In the VAB every rocket lists its payload to TLI, trans-lunar injection: what it can send toward the Moon. The first rockets, from the R-7 to the Atlas, read 0 kg there. An extra upper stage changes that: the R-7 built for the Luna probes sends 390 kg, the Saturn V 47 tonnes.

sheets.title: Why the Moon rocket is so big

points.title: Fuel to carry fuel
points.text: Each extra km/s multiplies the size of the rocket instead of adding to it, because the propellant for the last leg has to be lifted by every leg before it. An orbital rocket is already about 96% propellant; for the Moon, its payload is mostly another rocket.

points.title: Split the spacecraft
points.text: Landing one big ship on the Moon and flying it home would have needed an even larger rocket. Apollo landed only a light lander while the command ship waited in lunar orbit, and the two met again before going home. NASA engineer John Houbolt argued hard for this plan, and it fit the whole trip on one Saturn V.

points.title: Big, and still a gamble
points.text: A Saturn V weighed about 2,900 t at liftoff, some 24 times the Atlas that flew America's first orbital missions. The Soviet N1, almost as big, flew four times between 1969 and 1972 and failed every time.

sheets.inGame: Rockets come in classes, and a bigger class needs a higher VAB level before you can open it. The first rockets are all Light; the Moon rockets, the Saturn V and the N1, are Heavy.

explainers.title: Restarting in space
explainers.summary: Why lighting a rocket engine after a coast is hard when the propellant floats, and the three ways engineers solved it.

sheets.title: Fuel with no down

points.title: Everything falls together
points.text: While a spacecraft coasts, it and everything inside it are falling at the same rate, so nothing settles. Propellant breaks into floating blobs, creeps along the tank walls and sloshes at the slightest nudge.

points.title: Pumps want liquid, not gas
points.text: A big engine's pumps spin very fast and need a steady column of liquid. A gulp of gas can make them race out of control or starve the engine as it starts. Some engines can be lit only a few times, or only once, so a bad start may be the last chance.

points.title: Nudge, then light
points.text: The cure is a settling burn: small rockets fire for a few seconds to push the craft forward, the propellant drifts back to the bottom of its tanks, and only then does the main engine start. The Saturn V's third stage did this before it relit to leave Earth orbit for the Moon.

sheets.inGame: The R-7 lights every engine on the ground for this reason: in the early 1950s nobody knew whether a big engine could be started reliably high up. Its history note tells the story.

sheets.title: Three ways to a sure restart

points.title: Simple engines restart best
points.text: An engine fed by gas pressure has no pumps to starve, and propellants that ignite the moment they meet need no spark. Apollo's service module engine, which took the crew into lunar orbit and out again, was built this way. So was the lunar module's ascent engine, which had no backup.

points.title: Learned the hard way
points.text: Several of the first Soviet probes to Venus and Mars, in 1961 and 1962, never left Earth orbit: their top stage had to start after a coast in orbit, and it failed. On one, in August 1962, a small settling rocket didn't fire and the stage tumbled. Starting an engine in weightlessness took years of trial and error.

points.title: Every fix has a price
points.text: Self-igniting propellants are poisonous and attack seals. Gas-fed engines need heavy, thick-walled tanks. Bags and screens add weight and can wear out. Engineers pick the trade that fits: the more an engine must restart, the simpler it is built.

sheets.inGame: Retrofire is a start in space too, and Vostok's single retrorocket can't be fired twice. A step's odds rest on the reliability of the parts it uses; Payload R&D in the SET Centre raises it.

explainers.title: Hypergolics and steering jets
explainers.summary: Propellants that light the moment they touch, and the small jets that turn, slide and stop a spacecraft.

sheets.title: Fuels that light themselves

points.title: Two liquids, one flame
points.text: Hypergolic means a fuel and an oxidiser that burst into flame the instant they touch: no spark, no igniter, nothing to fail. Open two valves and the engine runs; close them and it stops. The word was coined by German rocket chemists in the 1940s.

points.title: Ready to wait
points.text: Liquid oxygen boils at −183 °C and must be topped up until the last minutes before launch. A hypergolic pair stays liquid at room temperature for months, so a missile can stand ready in its silo, and a spacecraft can wait days in orbit before its next burn.

points.title: The price is poison
points.text: The usual pair, a hydrazine fuel with nitrogen tetroxide, is toxic and eats through seals, so ground crews load it in sealed suits. In October 1960 an R-16 missile, fuelled with a similar self-igniting pair, exploded on its pad at Baikonur and killed at least 78 people.

sheets.inGame: The first rockets all burn liquid oxygen in their main stages, so each one is fuelled on launch day, and the Countdown step can still hold. Self-lighting propellants arrive with the Titan II and the Proton, both built as missiles that had to stand fuelled and ready.

sheets.title: Steering with small jets

points.title: Push one way, move the other
points.text: With no air there are no wings or fins to steer with. A reaction control system is a set of small rocket jets around the craft, usually grouped in fours. Each jet pushes the craft the opposite way to its exhaust.

points.title: Short, sharp and many
points.text: Steering jets fire in bursts of a fraction of a second, thousands of times on one flight. Self-lighting propellants suit them: there's nothing to ignite, only valves to open. The first capsules used simpler stuff: Vostok puffed cold nitrogen gas, Mercury broke down hydrogen peroxide.

points.title: Gemini 8's spin
points.text: In March 1966, just after the first docking, a jet on Gemini 8 stuck open. After undocking the capsule spun faster and faster, up to about one turn a second. Neil Armstrong shut the jets down and stopped the spin with the separate re-entry jets. Once those were used, the rules said come home, so the flight ended early.

sheets.inGame: The Reentry preparations step is steering-jet work: turning the capsule so its retrorockets point forward. On Faith 7, Gordon Cooper did it by hand, lining up on marks drawn on his window.

explainers.title: Falling, not floating
explainers.summary: Why a crew in orbit floats though gravity is still there, and what weeks of falling do to a body.

sheets.title: There is gravity in orbit

points.title: Gravity is still there
points.text: At 300 km up, Earth's gravity is still about nine-tenths as strong as on the ground. If it switched off, a spacecraft would fly away in a straight line instead of circling the Earth. Gravity is what holds it in orbit.

points.title: Everything falls together
points.text: A spacecraft in orbit is falling around the Earth, and so is everything inside it: the crew, the food, a loose pencil. Because they all fall at the same rate, nothing presses on anything else, and without that push you feel weightless.

points.title: “Zero g” means free fall
points.text: You feel a moment of it at the top of a swing or on a roller coaster's drop. Aircraft flying steep arcs give trainees about 25 seconds of it at a time. In orbit the fall simply never ends, so the feeling never stops.

sheets.inGame: The A day in orbit and Several days in orbit steps keep a crew falling around the Earth for a day or more.

sheets.title: What it does to a body

points.title: Could a person even swallow?
points.text: Before the first flights, doctors worried that without weight a person might not swallow, see straight or think clearly. Animals flew first. Gagarin ate paste from tubes on Vostok 1, and John Glenn squeezed apple sauce from a tube on his flight in 1962, just to be sure.

points.title: Titov's long day
points.text: In August 1961 Gherman Titov spent about 25 hours in orbit on Vostok 2. He was the first person to sleep in space, and the first to suffer space sickness: his inner ear and his eyes disagreed about which way was down.

points.title: Weeks bring weakness
points.text: With no weight to carry, muscles shrink and bones lose minerals, while fluids drift toward the head. Crews on long flights exercise every day, and still need time to walk steadily after landing: at first, even standing up can make them dizzy, because the heart has got used to pumping less hard.

sheets.inGame: Biometric data transmission sends a passenger's heartbeat and breathing home, and the Life in weightlessness goal asks you to fly living things in orbit and study how they cope.

explainers.title: Why capsules are blunt
explainers.summary: Why a blunt face beats a sharp nose coming home at 28,000 km/h, and how a shield survives the heat.

sheets.title: A blunt nose stays cooler

points.title: Speed becomes heat
points.text: Coming home from orbit, a capsule has to lose about 28,000 km/h. The air does the braking, and all that energy of motion turns into heat: the air piled up in front of the capsule glows at thousands of degrees.

points.title: A sharp nose cooks
points.text: A sleek, pointed nose cuts through the air, but the shock wave sits right on its tip and the hot air clings to its surface, so the heat flows into the craft. Make it hot enough and the nose melts. Early missile warheads had exactly this problem.

points.title: Allen's blunt body
points.text: In the early 1950s H. Julian Allen, an engineer at NACA's Ames laboratory, showed that a broad, blunt face works better. It pushes the shock wave out ahead, and most of the heat stays in that air and blows away. Every capsule since has been blunt.

sheets.inGame: The Reentry step is this moment: the capsule's blunt face takes the heat while the air brakes it from orbital speed.

sheets.title: How the shield survives

points.title: It burns so the capsule doesn't
points.text: Mercury's orbital capsules carried a heat shield of glass fibre and resin. As it heated, the resin boiled away from its outer layer, and the gases carried the heat off with them. A shield that is used up like this is called ablative. The suborbital capsules made do with a metal heat sink.

points.title: Radio silence
points.text: For a few minutes the air around the capsule is so hot that it glows and carries electricity, and radio signals can't get through it. On a Mercury flight this blackout lasted about four minutes, and Mission Control could only wait for the astronaut's voice to come back.

points.title: Eight times their weight
points.text: Braking that hard presses the crew into their seats with about eight times their normal weight. They lie on their backs, with the shield behind them, so the force pushes them into their couches and their blood isn't drained from their heads.

sheets.inGame: The Modules separation step frees the capsule from its equipment module before Reentry, so it can turn its shielded side forward.

explainers.title: The odds multiply
explainers.summary: Why small risks multiply over a mission's chain of steps, and how testing, backups and people fight them.

sheets.title: A chain of steps

points.title: Every step has to work
points.text: A flight is a chain of steps: countdown, launch, ascent, orbit, retrofire, re-entry, landing. Each one has to succeed for the mission to succeed, just as a chain is only as strong as its weakest link. If one fails, every step after it is lost too.

points.title: Small risks add up
points.text: Give each of 11 steps a 95 % chance and the whole flight succeeds only about 57 % of the time, not much better than a coin toss. Even at 99 % a step, about one flight in ten fails. Over a chain, chances multiply: 0.95 × 0.95 × … eleven times.

points.title: Not good enough for a person
points.text: A missile that works nine times in ten is a useful missile. A rocket that loses its crew one time in ten is unthinkable. That's why every part of a crewed flight is tested, doubled and checked until each step is very nearly certain.

sheets.inGame: Each step of a mission rolls on its own odds, and a failure that isn't rescued ends the mission. Vostok's and Mercury's orbital flights have 11 steps each.

sheets.title: Fighting the odds

points.title: Test it first
points.text: Before a person flew, each spacecraft and rocket flew empty, then with instruments or animals. The dogs Belka and Strelka orbited in August 1960, and Ham the chimpanzee rode a Mercury capsule in January 1961. Each test found faults that were fixed before a crew was on board.

points.title: Two of everything vital
points.text: A system that matters more than anything gets a backup. Vostok and Mercury each had an automatic way to aim the retrorockets and a manual one the pilot could use. If one failed, the other could still bring the crew home.

points.title: People catch what machines miss
points.text: Flight controllers watch every reading and know the spacecraft inside out. When something goes wrong, they can spot it, work out a fix and talk the crew through it. Some of the most famous rescues in spaceflight were made from the ground.

sheets.inGame: R&D raises a part's reliability, every program flies uncrewed test configurations before crewed ones, and when a step fails, your flight controllers' skill can still rescue it.

explainers.title: Getting out of a failing rocket
explainers.summary: Mercury's escape tower and Vostok's ejection seat, and the test flight where the tower saved a capsule.

sheets.title: Two answers to one danger

points.title: The most dangerous minutes
points.text: On the pad and in the first minutes of flight, a rocket is full of propellant and barely moving. If it fails then, it can explode in a fireball. A crew needs a way out that is faster than any explosion can spread.

points.title: Mercury's tower
points.text: Mercury carried a small solid rocket on a frame above the capsule. If the rocket below failed, the tower fired and pulled the whole capsule up and away in about a second, then dropped off so the parachutes could open.

points.title: Vostok's seat
points.text: Vostok had no tower. Its pilot sat in an ejection seat that could fire him out through a hatch if a launch failed early. The same seat ejected him at the end of every flight, and he landed under his own parachute.

sheets.inGame: The Launch step is one where the crew is at risk.

sheets.title: When it worked

points.title: Mercury-Atlas 3
points.text: In April 1961 an Atlas carrying an empty Mercury capsule failed to turn onto its planned path. About 40 seconds after liftoff the range safety officer destroyed it. The escape tower fired first and pulled the capsule clear. Nobody was aboard: this was one of the tests that came before a crewed Atlas flight.

points.title: The capsule flew again
points.text: The capsule came down under its parachutes, was picked up from the sea and flew again on the next Atlas test. An astronaut aboard would very likely have survived. The escape system had done exactly the job it was built for, at the worst possible moment.

points.title: Dropped when the danger is past
points.text: An escape tower is heavy, and every kilogram on top costs payload. Once the rocket's most dangerous minutes are over, about two and a half minutes into an Atlas flight, the tower is thrown away. From then on the crew relies on the rocket itself.

sheets.inGame: The Launch step is one where the crew is at risk, and its odds come from the rocket's and the capsule's reliability and the crew's skill. When it fails, your flight controllers' skill can still rescue it.

explainers.title: Land or sea
explainers.summary: Parachutes in stages, and why America came down at sea while the Soviet Union landed on the steppe.

sheets.title: Parachutes in stages

points.title: One parachute isn't enough
points.text: A capsule falls through the upper air at hundreds of kilometres an hour. A big parachute opened then would tear, or jerk the crew too hard. So a small drogue chute opens first to steady and slow the capsule, and the main chute opens lower down.

points.title: Mercury: into the sea
points.text: Mercury came down in the ocean, where ships and helicopters waited. Before splashdown its heat shield dropped about a metre on a rubber skirt; air filled the skirt through holes in it, making a landing bag that softened the blow as the capsule hit the water.

points.title: Vostok: two landings
points.text: Vostok's ball landed on the ground, too hard for a person inside. At about 7 km its hatch blew off and the pilot was ejected in his seat, then came down under his own parachute, a few kilometres from his spacecraft.

sheets.inGame: A Mercury flight ends with the Descent and splashdown step, a Vostok flight with Descent and landing.

sheets.title: Why each side chose its way

points.title: The sea
points.text: America had oceans on both sides and a large navy to search them. Water is a soft place to land, and ships and helicopters could wait near the target. The catch: a capsule had to float, and its crew had to get out safely.

points.title: The land
points.text: The Soviet Union had vast, empty steppes and few ships far from home. Landing on its own territory also kept the spacecraft secret. But the ground is hard, which is why Vostok's pilot came down on his own parachute.

points.title: Liberty Bell 7
points.text: In July 1961 Gus Grissom splashed down after the second crewed Mercury flight. The hatch blew off too early, the capsule filled with water, and Grissom nearly drowned before a helicopter picked him up. The capsule sank; it was raised from the ocean floor in 1999.

sheets.inGame: However you come home, the last step still rolls on the capsule's reliability and the crew's skill: Descent and landing for Vostok, Descent and splashdown for Mercury.

explainers.title: Talking to an orbiting craft
explainers.summary: Why the ground hears an orbiting craft only for minutes at a time, and how a network of stations follows it.

sheets.title: Only while it's in sight

points.title: Radio goes in straight lines
points.text: Radio waves travel in straight lines, like light. A ground station can only talk to a spacecraft while it is above the station's horizon. Once the craft drops below it, the Earth itself is in the way, and a craft over the far side of the world can't be reached at all.

points.title: A few minutes per pass
points.text: A craft in low orbit races across the sky. About 200 km up, it stays above one station's horizon for at most about seven minutes. Then it is gone for the rest of its 88-minute lap, and the next pass may be far off to one side.

points.title: So, many stations
points.text: One station hears a craft only briefly. To follow a flight around the world you need stations spread across continents and oceans, each handing the craft on to the next. Even then, Mercury's orbital flights had stretches where no station could hear the capsule.

sheets.inGame: The Orbital flight step is a craft falling around the Earth, in touch with the ground only for a few minutes at a time as it passes over a station.

sheets.title: A network around the world

points.title: A ring of stations
points.text: For Mercury, NASA built a network of tracking stations on land around the world, plus two ships, linked to Mission Control by telephone and teletype. Even so, a capsule spent part of every lap out of touch.

points.title: Anyone could listen
points.text: Sputnik 1 sent a simple beep on frequencies that radio amateurs could pick up. People all over the world heard it and recorded it. Launched on 4 October 1957, it beeped for about three weeks. The beeping made the first satellite impossible to doubt.

points.title: The pitch gives away the orbit
points.text: A passing satellite's signal sounds higher as it comes closer and lower as it leaves, like a passing siren. Two physicists at Johns Hopkins measured this change in Sputnik's signal and worked out its orbit. Turned around, the same trick became the first satellite navigation system.

sheets.inGame: The Radio from orbit goal asks for a satellite that broadcasts from orbit to the ground, as Sputnik 1 did; it's reached in the Earth orbit step.

explainers.title: What Explorer 1 found
explainers.summary: How a silent Geiger counter on Explorer 1 revealed the radiation belts, and why they matter.

sheets.title: Belts of radiation

points.title: A counter that went quiet
points.text: Explorer 1, launched in January 1958, carried a Geiger counter to count cosmic rays. On the high parts of its orbit, the count dropped to nothing. Either space was strangely empty up there, or something was wrong. Its readings only came down as it passed over a ground station, in short scraps.

points.title: Silence meant too much
points.text: James Van Allen's team at the University of Iowa realised the counter wasn't idle: it was swamped by so many particles that it stopped counting, like a microphone overloaded by a roar. Explorer 3, two months later, confirmed it.

points.title: Trapped by the magnetic field
points.text: Earth's magnetic field catches charged particles from the Sun and from space and holds them in two doughnut-shaped belts around the planet. The inner belt holds mostly protons, the outer one mostly electrons. They are named the Van Allen belts, after the scientist who explained them.

sheets.inGame: Explorer 1's flights reach the Space environment measured goal.

sheets.title: Why it matters

points.title: Harmful to crews
points.text: The trapped particles carry enough energy to damage living cells. A quick pass through the belts can be survived, but a crew that stayed inside them would soon take a dangerous dose. Astronauts carried badges that recorded the dose each of them received.

points.title: Crewed flights stay low
points.text: Vostok and Mercury flew a few hundred kilometres up, well beneath the inner belt. Later, Apollo crews crossed the belts on their way to the Moon, quickly and on a path that skirted the worst of them.

points.title: Know it, then design for it
points.text: Radiation upsets electronics too: one particle can flip a bit in a memory, and many slowly wear a part out. Knowing where the radiation is lets engineers choose safe orbits, add shielding and pick sturdier parts.

sheets.inGame: The Space environment measured goal stands for knowledge every later spacecraft design depends on.

explainers.title: Safe enough for a person
explainers.summary: What changes when a missile becomes a rocket for people, and how Mercury-Atlas earned its first crew.

sheets.title: From missile to crew launcher

points.title: A missile can afford to fail
points.text: A military missile only has to work most of the time: if one in ten fails, another is launched. A rocket carrying a person can't be treated that way, so the same rocket has to be changed before a crew may ride it.

points.title: Sense trouble, get out
points.text: The most important change is a system that watches the rocket. If an engine falters or the rocket starts to tumble, it shuts the engine down and fires the escape system faster than any person could react.

points.title: Mercury's Redstone
points.text: NASA took the Army's Redstone missile, lengthened its tanks so it could burn longer, added an abort-sensing system and strengthened parts that might fail. The changes turned a reliable missile into a rocket trusted with Alan Shepard in May 1961.

sheets.inGame: Only human-rated rockets can be assigned to crewed launches.

sheets.title: Earning trust

points.title: Flown before it carried anyone
points.text: Before John Glenn flew on an Atlas in February 1962, Mercury-Atlas had flown five times without a crew. Two of those flights failed and three succeeded, the last of them carrying the chimpanzee Enos around the Earth twice.

points.title: Every failure taught something
points.text: When the first Mercury-Atlas broke up in July 1960, engineers found the top of the rocket flexing and added a steel band to stiffen it. Each failure was traced, fixed and tested again before the next flight.

points.title: A record, not a promise
points.text: Human-rated doesn't mean a rocket can't fail. It means it has a record of flights and fixes that convinced people to trust it with a crew, and a way out if it fails anyway. Even today, every new crewed rocket flies without a crew first.

sheets.inGame: Only human-rated rockets can be assigned to crewed launches, and every program flies its uncrewed test configurations before its crewed ones.

explainers.title: Earth's free push
explainers.summary: Why rockets launch east, why the equator helps, and why Baikonur's orbits were tilted so steeply.

sheets.title: Launch east

points.title: The ground is already moving
points.text: Earth turns once a day, and the ground turns with it. At the equator that's about 465 m/s, almost 1,700 km/h, toward the east. A rocket standing on the pad is already moving that fast before it lights its engines.

points.title: Launch east to keep it
points.text: A rocket launched toward the east keeps that speed, and only has to add the rest of the 7.8 km/s it needs for orbit. Launched west, it would first have to cancel the Earth's spin, and then make up the whole of it.

points.title: Closer to the equator, a bigger push
points.text: Away from the equator the ground moves more slowly, because it turns in a smaller circle. Cape Canaveral, at 28.5° north, gets about 410 m/s; Baikonur, at about 46° north, only about 320 m/s. A site near the equator, like Europe's in French Guiana, gets almost the full push.

sheets.inGame: In Launch Window every rocket flies from its own side's site: an R-7 never launches from Florida, an Atlas never from Baikonur. So the VAB's LEO payloads, what each real rocket lifted from home, already include this push.

sheets.title: Where the rocket can go

points.title: An orbit circles the centre
points.text: Every orbit goes around the centre of the Earth. A rocket launched due east from 28.5° north ends up in an orbit tilted 28.5° to the equator. It can choose a steeper tilt, but never a shallower one without a costly turn.

points.title: Baikonur's steep orbits
points.text: Vostok's orbits were tilted about 65°. Baikonur couldn't launch due east, because the spent stages would have fallen on China, so its rockets flew north-east and got less of the Earth's push.

points.title: Over the sea, or empty land
points.text: A rocket drops its empty stages on the way up. Florida launches east over the Atlantic, so the stages fall into the ocean. Baikonur sits in a huge, thinly peopled steppe, and the zones where stages fall are cleared.

sheets.inGame: Vostok's R-7 and Mercury's Atlas lifted their real payloads from their own sites, and those are the payloads the VAB shows: the site's latitude is already counted in every rocket's lift.

explainers.title: The hardest moment of the climb
explainers.summary: The moment about a minute into a launch when the air pushes on a rocket hardest.

sheets.title: The hardest moment of the climb

points.title: Speed against thick air
points.text: As a rocket climbs it goes faster, and the faster it goes the harder the air pushes on it. But it also climbs into thinner air, which pushes less. For the first minute the speed wins; after that the thinning air does.

points.title: The peak: max Q
points.text: Engineers call that push dynamic pressure, written q, and its peak max Q. It comes about a minute after liftoff, roughly 10 to 15 km up, when the rocket's structure is squeezed and shaken hardest. Some rockets throttle down to get through it.

points.title: Mercury-Atlas 1
points.text: In July 1960 the first Atlas carrying a Mercury capsule broke up about a minute after liftoff, close to max Q. The top of the rocket had flexed too much where it met the capsule. A steel band was added to stiffen it, and later flights came through.

sheets.inGame: The Ascent step is the climb through max Q, and its odds rest mostly on the rocket's reliability.

explainers.title: Batteries and sunlight
explainers.summary: From batteries that ran down in weeks to solar cells that ran for years, and the nights every lap.

sheets.title: A satellite's power budget

points.title: Batteries run down
points.text: The first satellites carried batteries, like a torch. Sputnik 1's radio fell silent after about three weeks, though the satellite itself stayed in orbit for three months. Once its batteries were flat, a satellite was just a silent piece of metal.

points.title: Power from sunlight
points.text: Solar cells turn sunlight straight into electricity. The silicon kind had been invented at Bell Labs only four years earlier. Vanguard 1, launched in March 1958, carried six small panels of them. Its battery-powered radio stopped within months, but the solar-powered one kept transmitting until 1964.

points.title: Years instead of weeks
points.text: With solar cells a satellite could work for years, and that made weather, communication and navigation satellites worth building. Vanguard 1 is still in orbit today, the oldest human-made object up there, and is expected to stay up for centuries more.

sheets.inGame: “Extended mission” configurations carry more battery capacity, and they're the ones with an Extended experiments in orbit step.

sheets.title: Day and night in orbit

points.title: Night every 90 minutes
points.text: A satellite in low orbit goes round in about 90 minutes, so it passes through Earth's shadow about 16 times a day. On some orbits that's up to about 40 % of every lap with no sunlight at all.

points.title: Solar power needs batteries
points.text: Solar cells only work in sunlight. So a solar-powered spacecraft still carries batteries: it charges them on the sunny part of each lap and runs on them through the night. Over a long mission they are charged and drained thousands of times.

points.title: Hot, then cold
points.text: With no air to spread heat around, the side facing the Sun gets very hot and the shaded side very cold, and every pass into shadow swings the temperature again. Spacecraft are wrapped in shiny blankets and painted in patterns to keep their insides comfortable.

sheets.inGame: “Extended mission” configurations carry more battery capacity than the standard ones.

explainers.title: Keeping a rocket pointed
explainers.summary: Why a rocket must be steered every moment, and how Jupiter-C's spinning stages flew straight without steering.

sheets.title: Balancing on a flame

points.title: A rocket wants to tip over
points.text: A rocket pushes from the bottom, like a hand pushing a broom up from underneath. Left alone it starts to tip, and the tip grows. It has to be steered every moment, just to keep flying straight, and a small error early on grows into a big miss later.

points.title: Push the exhaust sideways
points.text: To steer, a rocket points part of its push slightly off centre. The Redstone put heat-proof vanes into its exhaust, like a rudder in water; the R-7 used small extra engines on swivels, called verniers; later rockets tilted the whole engine.

points.title: A guide inside
points.text: Gyroscopes inside the rocket sense the slightest turn, and the guidance system answers with a correction, many times a second. Without that constant correction, no large rocket could stay on its path for more than a few seconds.

sheets.inGame: The Ascent step rolls mostly on the rocket's reliability: steering errors there decide whether the payload reaches the planned orbit.

sheets.title: Spinning to fly straight

points.title: Spin holds direction
points.text: A spinning object resists being tipped over. A spinning top stays upright, and a rifle bullet, spun by grooves in the barrel, flies straight. Spin gives a rocket stability without any steering at all. The gyroscopes that sense a rocket's turns work on the same effect.

points.title: Jupiter-C's spinning tub
points.text: Jupiter-C's upper stages were small solid rockets: 11 in a ring, 3 inside them and 1 on top, all held in a tub that was spun up by an electric motor before launch. With no steering of their own, there was nothing in them to go wrong.

points.title: Aim first, then fire
points.text: The stage below did the steering. It carried the tub up and tipped it level, and after a coast the spinning stages fired one after another along the line they had been aimed. That is how Explorer 1 reached orbit in January 1958.

sheets.inGame: Jupiter-C lifts just enough to put Explorer 1 into orbit. Its Ascent step, like every rocket's, rolls mostly on the rocket's reliability.

explainers.title: Why satellites fall
explainers.summary: Why satellites in low orbit fall back, why height buys time, and how the Sun speeds the fall.

sheets.title: Thin air, long drag

points.title: A trace of air
points.text: Even 200 to 400 km up there is still a trace of air, billions of times thinner than at the ground. A satellite racing through it at 7.8 km/s bumps into enough of it to slow down, very slightly, on every lap.

points.title: Slower means lower
points.text: Slowing down lowers the orbit, and a lower orbit meets thicker air, which slows it more. The fall speeds up until the satellite drops into the thick air and burns up. Sputnik 1's big, light rocket stage felt more drag for its weight, and came down a month before the satellite.

points.title: Height buys time
points.text: Sputnik 1 dipped to about 215 km on each lap and fell after three months, in January 1958. Explorer 1, which never came lower than about 358 km, stayed up until 1970. A few hundred kilometres of height can mean weeks or centuries.

sheets.inGame: You fly Sputnik 1 and Explorer 1 in Launch Window. The real ones stayed up long after their radios fell silent: Sputnik 1 for about two more months, Explorer 1 for nearly twelve years.

sheets.title: The Sun stirs the air

points.title: The Sun heats the top of the air
points.text: The highest layers of the atmosphere are heated by ultraviolet light and X-rays from the Sun. When the Sun is active, with many sunspots and flares, it heats them more and they swell outward. The Sun goes from quiet to active and back about every 11 years.

points.title: Swollen air, stronger drag
points.text: At a satellite's height the air can become several times denser while the Sun is active. Drag rises, and orbits sink faster than expected. During a burst of solar activity in March 1989, so many objects dropped lower than predicted that trackers lost sight of hundreds of them for days.

points.title: Skylab came down early
points.text: The American space station Skylab was expected to stay up into the 1980s. A busy Sun in the late 1970s swelled the upper air, and Skylab fell in July 1979, before a planned Space Shuttle visit could boost it higher.

sheets.inGame: Launch Window doesn't model drag: a flight ends with its last step. The real Sputnik 1 and Explorer 1 came down when the air caught up with them.

explainers.title: A rocket held up by its own pressure
explainers.summary: How the Atlas saved weight with steel skin thinner than a millimetre, held in shape by its own pressure.

sheets.title: A rocket held up by its own pressure

points.title: Every kilogram counts
points.text: Every kilogram of tank, frame or wiring is a kilogram less that a rocket can carry. The Atlas was designed as a missile that had to throw a heavy warhead across the world, so its builders cut its weight wherever they could.

points.title: Held up by pressure
points.text: So the Atlas had no frame inside. Its tanks were its body: stainless steel, mostly thinner than a millimetre, held in shape by the pressure of the gas inside, like a balloon, or an unopened drink can, which is surprisingly hard to crush.

points.title: Never let it go flat
points.text: Even standing on the pad, an empty Atlas had to be kept pressurised, or it would crumple under its own weight. The trick made the Atlas very light for its size, and strong enough to put the first Americans into orbit.

sheets.inGame: Atlas is in the VAB, and its history note tells the story of its thin steel skin.

explainers.title: Three ways to the Moon
explainers.summary: Direct ascent, Earth-orbit rendezvous or lunar-orbit rendezvous: three ways to land on the Moon, and why the small lander won.

sheets.title: Three routes to the Moon

points.title: One giant rocket
points.text: Direct ascent is the simplest plan. One rocket sends the whole ship to the Moon, where it lands tail first, with enough fuel to take off again and fly home. Simple, but the rocket it needs would have been far bigger than anything ever built.

points.title: Two launches, one ship
points.text: Earth-orbit rendezvous splits the load. Two smaller rockets put the parts into Earth orbit, where they dock, and the assembled ship goes on to the Moon. Smaller rockets, but it needed a docking in orbit, which nobody had yet done.

points.title: Leave the ship in lunar orbit
points.text: Lunar-orbit rendezvous sends one ship and leaves most of it circling the Moon. A small lander goes down, comes back up and docks with the mothership, which brings the crew home. One rocket is enough, but the docking happens 380,000 km from home.

sheets.inGame: The Gemini Direct Ascent, Gemini EOR and Apollo programs fly these three routes.

sheets.title: Why the small lander won

points.title: Every kilogram is paid for twice
points.text: Whatever lands needs fuel to brake on the way down and more fuel to climb back up. Leaving the heat shield, the return engine and their fuel in lunar orbit made the landed craft a fraction of the weight, and one rocket could launch the lot.

points.title: Houbolt's campaign
points.text: John Houbolt, an engineer at NASA's Langley centre, pushed for lunar-orbit rendezvous when most of NASA thought a docking so far from home too risky. He wrote over his managers' heads to make the case. NASA chose it in July 1962.

points.title: Two Soviet answers
points.text: Korolev's N1-L3 also used lunar-orbit rendezvous, with a lander for one cosmonaut, the LK, who would have crossed to it from the orbiter by spacewalk. Chelomey's rival plan, the UR-700 rocket and the LK-700, would have landed directly. Neither ever carried a cosmonaut to the Moon.

sheets.inGame: The Soyuz 7K-L3 lunar landing program flies the LK, the LK-700 Direct Ascent program the LK-700. Whatever lands has to come back up: the Lunar ascent step.

explainers.title: Docking
explainers.summary: How two craft join in orbit, by hand or by radar, and how crews move across: through a tunnel or outside.

sheets.title: The last hundred metres

points.title: Park, then creep
points.text: After a rendezvous the two craft fly side by side, a few dozen metres apart, matching speed. Then the chaser creeps in along a straight line, slower than walking pace, with small puffs of its thrusters. Too fast, and the bump bounces them apart or damages both.

points.title: A probe and a cone
points.text: Apollo and Soyuz docked with a probe on one craft and a cone, the drogue, on the other. The cone guides the probe to its centre even if the aim is a little off. Small latches catch it, then the craft are pulled together and locked tight.

points.title: By hand or by machine
points.text: Neil Armstrong and David Scott docked Gemini 8 by hand with an Agena target in March 1966, the first docking ever. In October 1967 two uncrewed Soviet craft, Kosmos 186 and 188, docked on their own, steered by the Igla radar system.

sheets.inGame: The Igla docking system lets a craft dock with no crew on board. Dockings happen in steps such as Approach and docking and Automatic docking.

sheets.title: Turning around, and moving across

points.title: Transposition
points.text: Apollo's lunar module rode to space inside the top of the rocket's third stage, below the command ship. On the way to the Moon the command ship separated, turned around, docked nose to nose with the lander and pulled it out of the stage.

points.title: Through the tunnel
points.text: Once two craft are docked, the crew can take out the probe and the drogue. That opens a tunnel between the hatches, and the crew float from one craft to the other without suits.

points.title: Or outside
points.text: Soyuz 4 and 5 docked in January 1969, but their docking gear had no tunnel. So two cosmonauts put on suits and climbed across outside, and landed in a different craft from the one they had launched in.

sheets.inGame: Apollo's Transposition and docking step, and the Crew transfer step that moves people between docked craft.

explainers.title: Spacewalks
explainers.summary: Why a pressurised suit fights every move, how Leonov nearly couldn't get back in, and how Gemini learned to work outside.

sheets.title: A balloon shaped like a person

points.title: Pressure makes a suit stiff
points.text: In a vacuum a suit has to hold air around the body, at about a third of normal air pressure, in pure oxygen. The whole suit swells like a balloon, and every bend of an arm or grip of a glove is a fight against it.

points.title: Leonov's walk
points.text: On 18 March 1965 Alexei Leonov left Voskhod 2 through an inflatable airlock, the first person outside a spacecraft. After about 12 minutes his suit had swollen so much that he could not get back in. He let air out of it, against the rules, and squeezed in head first.

points.title: Why not more pressure?
points.text: A suit at full air pressure would be too stiff to move in. A suit at low pressure means breathing pure oxygen beforehand to flush nitrogen from the blood, or bubbles form, as in a diver's bends.

sheets.inGame: The Voskhod capsule carries an airlock for the Spacewalk step. The Berkut and Yastreb spacesuits are the Soviet suits for it.

sheets.title: Learning to work outside

points.title: Harder than it looked
points.text: Ed White's walk on Gemini 4 in June 1965 looked easy. A year later, on Gemini 9, Gene Cernan had nothing to hold on to: every push sent him drifting. His heart raced, sweat fogged his visor, and he came back in exhausted.

points.title: Handholds and practice
points.text: For Gemini 12 in November 1966, Buzz Aldrin had handholds and foot restraints, rested often, and had rehearsed underwater, where floating feels much like weightlessness. He worked outside for more than five hours over three outings.

points.title: Suits that carry their own air
points.text: Gemini suits hung on a hose to the capsule. Lunar suits carried a backpack with oxygen and cooling water. The Soviet Krechet opened at the back: the cosmonaut climbed in through a door that the backpack closed.

sheets.inGame: Each spacesuit, such as the Gemini spacesuit, Apollo lunar surface suit and Krechet lunar suit, is a component with its own R&D before a spacewalk.

explainers.title: Launch windows
explainers.summary: The cheapest path to Mars and Venus, and why it opens only every two years or so.

sheets.title: The cheapest way across

points.title: Coast, don't drive
points.text: No rocket can burn all the way to Mars. It burns for a few minutes to leave Earth, and then the probe coasts for months on a path around the Sun, falling freely like a thrown ball.

points.title: Touch both orbits
points.text: The cheapest path is half an ellipse around the Sun that just touches Earth's orbit where you leave and the target's orbit where you arrive. Walter Hohmann worked it out in 1925. It takes about 259 days to Mars and about 146 to Venus.

points.title: Aim where it will be
points.text: You don't aim at Mars but at where Mars will be when you get there. So at launch Mars has to be about 44° ahead of Earth, and that happens only once in a while.

sheets.inGame: The Earth departure step is the burn, and the Cruise to Mars and Cruise to Venus steps are the long coast.

sheets.title: Why you wait

points.title: The line-up comes round again
points.text: Earth goes round the Sun faster than Mars, like a runner on the inside lane, and laps it about every 26 months. Venus, on the inside of Earth, laps it about every 19 months. Only then are the planets lined up for the cheap path.

points.title: A window, then a wait
points.text: For a few weeks around each line-up a launch costs little extra. Outside it the trip needs far more fuel than any rocket could give. That stretch of weeks is a launch window: miss it, and you wait two years for the next.

points.title: Everyone goes at once
points.text: So everyone launches in the same weeks. In May 1971 five craft left for Mars. Mariner 8 was lost at launch and Kosmos 419 never left Earth orbit, but Mariner 9, Mars 2 and Mars 3 all arrived that winter.

sheets.inGame: Planetary missions take several seasons: the launch, then the cruise, then the approach. And a launch window gives the game its name.

explainers.title: Gravity assists
explainers.summary: How a probe borrows a planet's speed for free, and how Mariner 10 and Pioneer 11 used it.

sheets.title: Borrowing a planet's speed

points.title: From the planet, nothing gained
points.text: A probe falls toward a planet, swings round it and climbs away again. Seen from the planet, it leaves exactly as fast as it came. Only its direction has changed.

points.title: From the Sun, a free push
points.text: But the planet itself is racing round the Sun. Seen from the Sun, its motion adds to the probe's, so the probe can leave much faster than it came, or slower if it passes in front. It costs no fuel at all.

points.title: A ball off a train
points.text: Throw a ball at the front of an oncoming train and it bounces back faster than you threw it, because it picks up the train's speed. A flyby does the same with gravity instead of a bounce.

sheets.inGame: Flyby steps such as the Venus flyby and Jupiter flyby swing a probe on toward its next target.

sheets.title: Planet to planet

points.title: Venus first, then Mercury
points.text: Mariner 10 left Earth in November 1973 and swung past Venus in February 1974. Venus bent its path inward to Mercury: the first probe to use one planet to reach another.

points.title: Three passes for one
points.text: Its new orbit around the Sun took exactly two of Mercury's years, so it met Mercury again and again: in March 1974, September 1974 and March 1975, until its steering gas ran out.

points.title: Jupiter to Saturn
points.text: Pioneer 11 passed closer to Jupiter than any probe before, in December 1974. Jupiter's gravity flung it right across the solar system, and it reached Saturn in September 1979.

sheets.inGame: The Mariner 10 and Pioneer 11 programs fly these routes, with a Venus flyby or Jupiter flyby on the way.

explainers.title: Landing on other worlds
explainers.summary: Landing on the Moon with rockets alone, on Venus through crushing air, and on Mars with a bit of everything.

sheets.title: Rockets all the way down

points.title: Nothing to brake against
points.text: The Moon has no air, so a heat shield or a parachute would be no use at all. All the speed a lander carries has to be taken away by its engine, and every bit of it costs fuel.

points.title: Hard, then soft
points.text: Ranger probes were simply aimed at the Moon and sent pictures until they hit it at full speed. Luna 9 on 3 February 1966 and Surveyor 1 on 2 June 1966 braked with rockets and landed softly, which showed the ground would hold a lander up.

points.title: Fuel for the last metres
points.text: A crewed lander also needs fuel to hover while the pilot looks for a clear spot. On Apollo 11 Neil Armstrong flew on past a field of boulders, and the lander touched down with less than a minute of fuel to spare.

sheets.inGame: The Powered descent and Lunar landing steps bring a lander down, and the Lunar ascent step takes it back up.

sheets.title: Venus and Mars

points.title: Venus: far too much air
points.text: At the surface of Venus the air presses about 90 times harder than on Earth, as deep as 900 metres under the sea, at about 465 °C. Early probes were crushed on the way down. Venera 7 landed on 15 December 1970 and sent the first signal ever from another planet's surface.

points.title: Mars: not quite enough
points.text: The air on Mars is less than 1 % as thick as Earth's. That is enough to make a probe glow hot, so it still needs a heat shield, but too thin for a parachute alone to slow it to a safe landing.

points.title: Parachute, then rockets
points.text: So Mars landers use all three: a heat shield, then a parachute, then rockets for the last part. Mars 3 landed on 2 December 1971 and fell silent within seconds. Viking 1 landed on 20 July 1976 and worked for years.

sheets.inGame: The Large probe entry, Lander entry and Descent and landing steps bring probes down on Venus and Mars.

explainers.title: Far from home
explainers.summary: Why sunlight runs out for the outer probes, and how radio reaches them across the solar system.

sheets.title: Sunlight runs out

points.title: Sunlight thins with distance
points.text: Twice as far from the Sun, a solar panel catches a quarter of the light. At Jupiter it gets about 4 % of what it would at Earth, so a probe would need enormous panels to run at all.

points.title: Power from heat
points.text: So the outer probes carried radioisotope generators. A lump of plutonium stays hot for decades as it decays, and the generator turns that heat straight into electricity, with no moving parts. Pioneer 10 and 11 carried them, and so did the Viking landers on Mars.

points.title: Keeping warm through the night
points.text: A lunar night lasts about two weeks. The Lunokhod rover ran on solar panels by day, and at night it closed its lid and kept its insides warm with a small radioactive heater.

sheets.inGame: The Pioneer 10 and Pioneer 11 probes and the Viking lander carry their own power source.

sheets.title: Talking across the solar system

points.title: Light takes time
points.text: Radio travels at the speed of light. A signal from the Moon takes about 1.3 seconds, and one from Mars between about 3 and 22 minutes, depending on where the planets are. Nobody can steer a probe out there by hand as it happens.

points.title: A whisper and a big ear
points.text: A probe's radio is about as strong as a light bulb, and by the time it reaches Earth the signal is unimaginably faint. Dishes tens of metres across collect it. Three stations, in California, Spain and Australia, keep one in view as the Earth turns.

points.title: Driving with a delay
points.text: Lunokhod 1 landed in November 1970 and was driven from a control room on Earth by a crew of five, watching slow TV pictures. Each order reached the rover seconds after it was given, so they drove carefully.

sheets.inGame: The Lunokhod rover is driven from Earth, and probe missions still need flight controllers in Mission Control.

explainers.title: Pictures before digital cameras
explainers.summary: How Luna 3 developed its film in space and radioed the far side of the Moon home.

sheets.title: Film, developed in space

points.title: No way to bring the film home
points.text: In 1959 there were no electronic cameras good enough to take a sharp picture. A probe could carry a film camera, but the film could never come back. So Luna 3 carried a tiny photo lab as well.

points.title: Develop, scan, transmit
points.text: On 7 October 1959 Luna 3 photographed the far side of the Moon. It developed, fixed and dried the film on board, then a small spot of light scanned each frame and the brightness was radioed home, line by line, like a fax.

points.title: Mapping for Apollo
points.text: Lunar Orbiter used the same idea in 1966 and 1967, with much finer film, to photograph the Moon in great detail from orbit. Its pictures helped choose where Apollo would land.

sheets.inGame: The Luna 3 and Lunar Orbiter programs photograph the Moon.

explainers.title: Moon rock by robot
explainers.summary: How Luna 16 drilled the Moon and flew a sample straight home, with no crew.

sheets.title: A piece of the Moon by robot

points.title: A drill on an arm
points.text: Luna 16 landed in the Sea of Fertility in September 1970. Its arm drilled about 35 cm into the ground, then swung round and dropped the core into a small sealed capsule on top of the lander.

points.title: Straight home
points.text: The top stage lifted off and flew straight back to Earth, with no rendezvous in lunar orbit. The capsule came down by parachute in Kazakhstan with about 100 grams of Moon soil, the first brought back without a crew.

points.title: The race that wasn't
points.text: Luna 15 tried first, in July 1969, while Apollo 11 was at the Moon. It crashed while coming down on 21 July, about two hours before Armstrong and Aldrin lifted off with their own samples.

sheets.inGame: The Luna 15 program tries for a sample return.

explainers.title: Rocket planes
explainers.summary: The X-15's flights to the edge of space, and the spaceplanes that lost to the capsules.

sheets.title: Rocket planes at the edge of space

points.title: Launched from a bomber
points.text: The X-15 rode under the wing of a B-52 bomber, dropped, lit its rocket and climbed almost straight up. It reached Mach 6.7, about 7,300 km/h, in 1967, and in 1963 Joe Walker flew it to about 108 km.

points.title: Steering where there's no air
points.text: Fins and flaps need air to push against. High up the air is too thin, so the X-15 had small thrusters in its nose and wings, the same trick capsules use. Its pilots learned to fly in space with them.

points.title: Wings or capsules
points.text: US pilots who flew above 50 miles, about 80 km, earned astronaut wings. Spaceplanes promised to land on a runway and fly again, and the Soviet Spiral project tested a small MiG spaceplane in the air. But in the 1960s the capsules won.

sheets.inGame: The X-15 and OKB-MiG E-154 programs launch from a carrier plane, in the Carrier takeoff and Drop and ignition steps: no rocket needed.

explainers.title: Around the Moon and back
explainers.summary: The figure-of-eight path that brings a crew home from the Moon with no burn, and the fast, narrow way back in.

sheets.title: The free return

points.title: A figure of eight
points.text: Aim just right when you leave Earth, and the Moon's gravity swings the craft round its far side and throws it back towards Earth. No more burns are needed to come home.

points.title: A way back built in
points.text: So if the engine fails after leaving Earth, the crew still comes home. Zond 5 flew this path in September 1968, with tortoises on board, the first living things to go round the Moon and come back. Apollo 8 set out on it too, before braking into lunar orbit.

points.title: Apollo 13
points.text: In April 1970 an oxygen tank exploded on Apollo 13's way to the Moon. The crew used the lunar module's engine to put the ship back on a free-return path, swung round the Moon and came home.

sheets.inGame: The Zond 5, Soyuz 7K-L1 circumlunar and Circumlunar Gemini programs fly around the Moon and home, and Apollo's lunar flybys swing round in the Around the Moon step.

sheets.title: Coming home fast

points.title: About 11 km/s
points.text: A craft coming back from the Moon hits the air at about 11 km/s, much faster than from Earth orbit. It has about twice as much energy to get rid of, so its heat shield has to be much tougher.

points.title: A narrow corridor
points.text: Come in too steeply and the braking and the heat are deadly. Come in too shallowly and the craft skims off the top of the air, back into space. The safe corridor is only a few degrees wide.

points.title: Skipping like a stone
points.text: Soviet Zond capsules dipped into the air, skipped back out, and came in a second time to land in the Soviet Union, more gently. Zond 7 in August 1969 was the first to do it all the way to a safe landing.

sheets.inGame: Lunar missions come home in the Approach and reentry step, and the Gemini lunar-speed reentry and Apollo lunar-speed reentry goals test the heat shield at that speed.
